# Rule reference

<!-- Generated by tests/integration/docs_test.go from the rule catalog. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every rule evaluates only the normalized snapshot. A rule returns SKIP when the data it needs could not be collected (unsupported platform, component not installed, insufficient privileges) and ERROR when collection or evaluation failed unexpectedly. None of these rules claims conformance with CIS Benchmarks or any other standard.

## SSH-001

**SSH root login with a password must not be allowed**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux, windows

PermitRootLogin yes lets anyone who knows or guesses the root password log in remotely as root.

*Why HIGH:* Direct password-based root login exposes the most privileged account to remote brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks and yields full system control on success.

*Remediation:* Set 'PermitRootLogin no' (or 'prohibit-password' if key-based root access is required) and reload sshd.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-002

**SSH root login should be disabled entirely**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: LOW
- Platforms: linux, windows

Any PermitRootLogin value other than 'no' allows remote root sessions (for example with keys), bypassing per-user accountability.

*Why LOW:* Key-based root login is not directly brute-forceable, so the residual risk is loss of accountability and a larger blast radius for a stolen key rather than an exploitable weakness.

*Remediation:* Set 'PermitRootLogin no'; administrators log in as themselves and elevate with sudo.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-003

**SSH password authentication should be disabled**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux, windows

PasswordAuthentication yes accepts passwords, which can be guessed, reused or phished, instead of requiring keys or certificates.

*Why MEDIUM:* Password login enables online guessing against every account, but exploitation still requires a weak or leaked password, so the impact is conditional.

*Remediation:* Deploy SSH keys for all users, then set 'PasswordAuthentication no'.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-004

**SSH keyboard-interactive authentication via PAM should be disabled**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux, windows

With UsePAM yes, keyboard-interactive authentication usually prompts for the account password, re-enabling password logins even when PasswordAuthentication is no.

*Why MEDIUM:* It is an equivalent path to password authentication and carries the same conditional risk of password guessing.

*Remediation:* Set 'KbdInteractiveAuthentication no' unless PAM is used for a second factor that requires it.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-005

**SSH must not permit empty passwords**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux, windows

PermitEmptyPasswords yes allows login to accounts that have no password at all.

*Why HIGH:* Any account with an empty password becomes remotely accessible without credentials; no guessing is required.

*Remediation:* Set 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' (the OpenSSH default) and lock or set passwords for such accounts.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-006

**SSH must not process user-supplied environment files**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux, windows

PermitUserEnvironment lets users set variables through ~/.ssh/environment or authorized_keys options, which can bypass restrictions such as ForceCommand (for example via LD_PRELOAD).

*Why MEDIUM:* Exploitation requires an authenticated user, but it can defeat restricted-shell and forced-command setups that the configuration relies on.

*Remediation:* Set 'PermitUserEnvironment no' (the OpenSSH default).

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-007

**SSH MaxAuthTries should be 4 or lower**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: LOW
- Platforms: linux, windows

MaxAuthTries limits authentication attempts per connection; high values make online guessing cheaper.

*Why LOW:* The setting only slows guessing per connection; attackers can reconnect, so the security gain is incremental.

*Remediation:* Set 'MaxAuthTries 4' or lower.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-008

**SSH X11 forwarding should be disabled**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: LOW
- Platforms: linux, windows

X11Forwarding exposes the client's X display to the server, where a compromised server can capture input or screen content.

*Why LOW:* The risk falls mainly on clients connecting to a compromised server and requires the client to request forwarding.

*Remediation:* Set 'X11Forwarding no' unless graphical forwarding is required.

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## SSH-009

**SSH must not enable weak ciphers, MACs or key exchange algorithms**

- Category: ssh
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux, windows

Explicit Ciphers, MACs or KexAlgorithms settings can re-enable algorithms that modern OpenSSH disables by default: CBC-mode and RC4 ciphers, MD5/truncated-SHA1/RIPEMD MACs and SHA-1 based key exchange.

*Why MEDIUM:* Practical attacks require a network position and, for most of these algorithms, significant effort, but they weaken the confidentiality or integrity guarantees of every session.

*Remediation:* Remove the listed algorithms from Ciphers, MACs and KexAlgorithms, or remove the directives to use the OpenSSH defaults (on RHEL-family systems adjust the system crypto policy instead).

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8758>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9142>

## USER-001

**Only root may have UID 0**

- Category: accounts
- Severity: CRITICAL
- Platforms: linux

Any account with UID 0 has full root privileges regardless of its name; additional UID 0 accounts are a common backdoor.

*Why CRITICAL:* An extra UID 0 account is equivalent to a second root account and typically indicates compromise or a severe misconfiguration.

*Remediation:* Remove the account or assign it a unique non-zero UID after investigating why it exists.

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html>

## USER-002

**Local accounts must not have empty passwords**

- Category: accounts
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux

An empty password field allows authentication without a password wherever null passwords are accepted (for example PAM with nullok).

*Why HIGH:* Access requires no secret at all; whether it is remotely exploitable depends on PAM and service configuration, which keeps it below CRITICAL.

*Remediation:* Lock the account ('passwd -l NAME') or set a strong password.

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/shadow.5.html>
- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html>

## USER-003

**Password hashes must not be stored in /etc/passwd**

- Category: accounts
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux

/etc/passwd is world-readable; a hash stored there instead of /etc/shadow can be copied and cracked offline by any local user.

*Why MEDIUM:* Requires local access and successful offline cracking, but exposes credentials to every local user.

*Remediation:* Run 'pwconv' to move hashes into /etc/shadow, then verify with 'pwck'.

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html>
- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/shadow.5.html>

## USER-004

**Local accounts must have unique UIDs**

- Category: accounts
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux

Accounts sharing a UID share file ownership and process privileges, which breaks accountability and access separation.

*Why MEDIUM:* Shared UIDs grant one account the other's access and hide who performed an action, but do not by themselves grant elevated privileges (UID 0 duplicates are covered by USER-001).

*Remediation:* Assign unique UIDs and fix file ownership with 'find / -uid OLD -exec chown NEW {} +'.

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html>

## USER-005

**System accounts should not have interactive login shells**

- Category: accounts
- Severity: LOW
- Platforms: linux

Service accounts (UID below UID_MIN) are not meant for interactive use; a login shell lets an attacker who obtains their credentials or keys get a shell.

*Why LOW:* Exploitation requires another weakness that grants authentication as the service account; the shell only widens what can be done afterwards.

*Remediation:* Set the shell to nologin ('usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin NAME'; the path is /sbin/nologin on RHEL-family systems) unless the account genuinely requires one.

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html>
- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/login.defs.5.html>

## FW-001

**A host firewall must filter inbound traffic**

- Category: firewall
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux, windows

Checks for evidence that inbound traffic is filtered: on Linux, a drop or reject reachable from an nftables input chain or a running firewalld; on Windows, Windows Defender Firewall enabled for all profiles with its service running.

*Why HIGH:* Without host filtering every listening service is reachable from every attached network; on flat or cloud networks the host firewall is often the only network-level control.

*Remediation:* Linux: enable firewalld ('systemctl enable --now firewalld'), ufw ('ufw enable') or an nftables ruleset with a default-deny input policy. Windows: enable the firewall for the Domain, Private and Public profiles ('Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -Enabled True').

*References:*

- <https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Main_Page>
- <https://firewalld.org/documentation/>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/network-security/windows-firewall/>

## FILE-001

**/etc/shadow must not be accessible to other users**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux

/etc/shadow contains password hashes; it must be owned by root, not group-writable and have no permissions for others.

*Why HIGH:* Read access exposes every password hash to offline cracking; write access allows setting any account's password, including root's.

*Remediation:* chown root /etc/shadow && chmod 0640 /etc/shadow (Debian family, group shadow) or chmod 0000 (RHEL family).

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/shadow.5.html>
- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html>

## FILE-002

**/etc/gshadow must not be accessible to other users**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux

/etc/gshadow contains group passwords and administrator lists; it must be owned by root with no permissions for others.

*Why MEDIUM:* Group passwords are rarely used, so exposure usually has less impact than /etc/shadow, but write access still allows joining privileged groups.

*Remediation:* chown root /etc/gshadow && chmod 0640 /etc/gshadow (or 0000 on RHEL-family systems).

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html>

## FILE-003

**/etc/passwd must be writable only by root**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: CRITICAL
- Platforms: linux

/etc/passwd defines UIDs and shells; it must be owned by root and not writable by group or others.

*Why CRITICAL:* Write access lets any user add a UID 0 account or change root's password field, an immediate and reliable privilege escalation.

*Remediation:* chown root:root /etc/passwd && chmod 0644 /etc/passwd

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html>
- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html>

## FILE-004

**/etc/group must be writable only by root**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux

/etc/group defines group membership, including administrative groups such as sudo or wheel.

*Why HIGH:* Write access lets a user join an administrative group and typically gain root through sudo on the next login.

*Remediation:* chown root:root /etc/group && chmod 0644 /etc/group

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html>

## FILE-005

**/etc/sudoers must be owned by root and not writable by others**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux

The sudoers policy decides who may run commands as root.

*Why HIGH:* Write access to the policy is a direct path to root; sudo refuses some unsafe modes, which limits but does not remove the risk.

*Remediation:* chown root:root /etc/sudoers && chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers (edit only with visudo).

*References:*

- <https://www.sudo.ws/docs/man/sudoers.man/>

## FILE-006

**/etc/ssh/sshd_config must be writable only by root**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: HIGH
- Platforms: linux

The SSH server configuration controls remote authentication.

*Why HIGH:* Write access allows weakening remote authentication for every account (for example enabling root login or empty passwords) the next time sshd reloads its configuration.

*Remediation:* chown root:root /etc/ssh/sshd_config && chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config

*References:*

- <https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config>

## FILE-007

**World-writable temporary directories must have the sticky bit**

- Category: file-permissions
- Severity: MEDIUM
- Platforms: linux

Without the sticky bit on /tmp and /var/tmp any user can delete or replace other users' files.

*Why MEDIUM:* Enables tampering with other users' temporary files and symlink races against privileged programs, which depends on a vulnerable program to become an escalation.

*Remediation:* chmod 1777 /tmp /var/tmp

*References:*

- <https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html>
